extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers, and commentators interested in cultural appropriation and related ethical/legal debates
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative dimensions for judging whether an instance of cross-cultural use counts as harmful cultural appropriation (versus benign cultural exchange, artistic practice, or innovation). Covers ethical, legal, historical, artistic, and economic considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disrespect over ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: "The key question in the use of symbols or regalia associated with another identity group is not: What are my rights of ownership? Rather it's: Are my actions disrespectful?" (Kwame Anthony Appiah)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the action by whether it is disrespectful to the source community rather than by property-rights metaphors. Apply this to use of symbols, regalia, hairstyles, dress, and other culturally significant items; consider whether the use conveys contempt or denigration. (Example: Appiah's framing shifts focus from 'who owns culture' to 'is this disrespectful?')

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish colonial exploitation vs appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Byung-Chul-Han distinguishes between "colonial exploitation" and appropriation, calling appropriation an "essential part of education and identity" and arguing that seeing appropriation as inherently "sinful" is derivative of certain humanities paradigms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging an instance, separate exploitative, extractive, or colonial power-driven uses from ordinary cultural borrowing or learning; do not collapse all cross-cultural contact into a single condemnable category. Consider historical power imbalances to identify exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid essentializing cultural difference / exclusive ownership claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of appropriation can "essentialize cultural difference" by implying that a supposedly appropriated element is the exclusive property of one group (Markus Tauschek).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of treating cultural elements as immutable, uniquely owned properties. Scrutinize claims that a style/practice is the exclusive property of a single group; consider hybridization, diffusion, and the non-static nature of culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for misuse of the term and cancel-culture effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular discourse sometimes misuses 'cultural appropriation' and can enable cancel culture (Ezedimbu et al.; Ash Sarkar called the term "an imperfect term mobilised in imperfect contexts").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether accusations are specific and justified or whether the term is being applied as a blunt tool to shame or silence. Consider motive, proportionality, and whether the response fosters constructive dialogue or mere public shaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider historical and structural context (imperialism, white supremacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics note that media conversations are often reductive and ignore the broader picture of imperial racism and white supremacy that forms the context for many controversies (Afua Hirsch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in the history of colonialism, systemic oppression, and power asymmetries when evaluating appropriative acts. The same act can carry different meanings depending on that history and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective consent and intellectual-property limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying intellectual property reasoning to cultural practices is complicated because some supposed cultural 'properties' belong to groups "too large to have any reliable mechanism that would operationalise ... a consent procedure"; IP frameworks do not map cleanly onto cultural claims (Mathias Siems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize legal and practical limits: who speaks for a culture, how to obtain consent, and whether IP mechanisms are workable. Avoid treating IP metaphors as simple solutions to ethical questions about culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blanket rejection — account for benefits of cultural mixing
rubrics_metrics.description: A general rejection of any form of cultural appropriation could be harmful for societies by impeding benefits of cultural mixing (Mathias Siems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance harms against potential benefits (innovation, hybrid forms, cross-cultural understanding). Not all borrowing is wrongful; evaluate consequences and whether exchange is reciprocal or one-sided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic freedom to imagine and write across cultures
rubrics_metrics.description: Several writers (Kenan Malik, Brian Morton, Kamila Shamsie, Lionel Shriver, Bernadine Evaristo) argue that authors and artists have a right to write/think in the voice of people outside their own culture; imaginative empathy and satirical/offensive writing have artistic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating creative work, weigh the value of imaginative practice, solidarity through imaginative effort, and the role of satire/offense against potential misrepresentation or harm. Consider whether constraints on artistic voice would unduly limit essential artistic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware minority-representative gatekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Malik warns that those who levy the charge of appropriation on behalf of minority communities can "appropriate for themselves the authority to license certain forms of cultural engagement," potentially entrenching power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question who is claiming the authority to police cultural boundaries and whether that policing itself creates exclusionary gatekeeping. Evaluate the legitimacy and representativeness of accusers or self-appointed cultural guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotyping, costumes, and derogatory portrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: Dressing up as 'another culture' can be racist and results in offensive, inaccurate, and stereotypical portrayals (e.g., imitation Native headdresses, Halloween costumes, mascots).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the portrayal reduces a culture to stereotypes or caricature, mocks sacred practices, or reinforces derogatory tropes. Examples cited include festival headdresses, racist college parties, and costume-related controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commodification and one-sided economic benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural sharing often yields one-sided benefits; rebranding or monetizing cultural products (e.g., food, fashion) can amount to culinary appropriation or gentrification (examples: 'spa water' vs agua fresca).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge commercial uses for whether origin communities are marginalized while others profit, whether naming/rebranding erases origins, and whether economic harms or cultural erasure result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacred/spiritual exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using sacred items or ceremonies (e.g., Native headdresses, sweat lodges, spiritual practices) as fashion or entertainment is described as embodiment of appropriation and can cause real harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sacred items/rituals with heightened care: determine whether use disrespects religious or spiritual significance, poses safety risks, or commodifies sacred practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate cultural change/diffusion from appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly work emphasizes delineating boundaries between genuine cultural change, diffusion, syncretism, and exploitative appropriation (Rogers; Kunst et al.; Cruz et al.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply criteria to determine whether a practice represents a natural process of cultural contact and adaptation or an exploitative one-sided taking. Look at directionality, reciprocity, power relations, and agency of source communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive racial presentation and identity performance (blackfishing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performative attempts to appear as another racial identity (blackfishing) involve deception and misrepresentation (examples: influencers accused of pretending to be Black).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess intent to deceive, the harms from misrepresentation, and whether the act appropriates markers of an oppressed group's identity for social/financial gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and complexity of group membership complicates ownership claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Some supposed cultural 'properties' (e.g., gendered practices, widely diffused traditions) are shared across groups so broadly that collective ownership or a single consent mechanism is impractical (Mathias Siems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims of group ownership arise, evaluate the meaningfulness of group boundaries, internal diversity, and whether a practicable consent or licensing regime exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question the 'identity-crime' framing and assumptions about belonging
rubrics_metrics.description: Walter Benn Michaels argues that both enthusiasm and disapproval of appropriation often rest on dubious distinctions between what we 'actually believe and do' and what we're 'supposed to believe and do', and criticizes the assumption of cultural 'belonging' that validates 'identity crimes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of frameworks that treat cultural crossing as a legalistic 'crime' of identity. Examine whether moral condemnation depends on rigid notions of belonging and whether such frameworks obscure more relevant social dynamics.
